command: pure Python, PyPI hocon2 0.6.3 (myjniak/hocon): parse the file, the tree as JSON

failures.rule: an object whose field a is itself a merge of an object and a substitution concatenates with a substituted object like any other: the two merge. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) because the concatenation is not registered as the merge's parent; the same objects written as literals concatenate fine

${a} in a's own value refers to the earlier a, an object, so the concatenation merges {p: ...} with {q: 1}; the inner p is itself a merge of an object and a substitution. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) when the merge inside a concatenation piece resolves, as in 018

inside each ${a} { ... } the undefined ${?missing} leaves the c before it, and the later b merges over the earlier one: c is 2; typesafe/config fails with an internal error (lightbend/config#647, #725, #754)
the later c, an object, overrides the string before it inside the object merged onto ${a}; typesafe/config fails with an internal error (lightbend/config#356)
${tail} is a list, so it concatenates with the list before it, whose object keeps foo = 1 under the undefined ${?bar}; typesafe/config fails with an internal error (lightbend/config#751)

${x} is x's object {q:2}; the 5 it overrode is x's history, not its value, so { p = 1 } ${x} merges into {p:1, q:2}. The rule of duplicate-keys-and-object-merging/029 reached through concatenation instead of a duplicate key; typesafe/config 1.4.9 lets the 5 cut the merge and keeps only {q:2}
U+200B is format (Cf), not a space separator, so it is text, and text between two list substitutions is invalid. typesafe/config drops it and concatenates the lists; lightbend/config#862 rejects it

the mirror of 008: an undefined optional substitution before an array becomes an empty array too. typesafe/config keeps the whitespace before the list as text and rejects it, while accepting 008 (noted on lightbend/config#862)

the object twin of 009: an undefined optional substitution before an object substitution becomes an empty object and the whitespace between them is ignored. typesafe/config keeps the whitespace before the object as text and rejects it, while accepting ${x} ${?absent}

the null at r only stops merging at r; ${r} is the object {x:1}, and a later object merges with the earlier a, so helper stays. typesafe/config carries r's null through the substitution and drops helper (lightbend/config#864)
the same rule one level down: the null in v.nested's history belongs to v.nested, so a.nested still merges with the substituted {x:1} (lightbend/config#864)

a substitution sees the resolved value of the field it names, so o24bbd equals a.nested, which keeps helper. The key name is chosen to sort before a in typesafe/config's root HashMap, the order in which the first version of lightbend/config#864 answered differently for the two
the null belongs to v's history even when v's object is still unresolved, so a merges and keeps helper (lightbend/config#864)

${r} is an object, so it merges with the earlier a and the ${missing} inside it is evaluated: an error. typesafe/config 1.4.5 agreed; 1.4.9 drops the earlier a and yields {y:1}, and lightbend/config#864 restores the error

v's value is a merge whose top is an object and whose null sits further down, under nested; that null is still v.nested's merge instruction, so a.nested keeps helper (lightbend/config#864 review, round 3)

two nested nulls each break only their own key's merge, and a lookup of a.n.d sees the final {x:1}; typesafe/config throws BugOrBroken in this key order (reported on lightbend/config#864, same on main)

the object replaces the earlier list, so a.m exists and p is 1 whatever order the keys are resolved in. typesafe/config fails when the reader p is resolved before a (it iterates p before a); the same file with the reader named zzz resolves

${x} is x's merged object {q:2}; the 5 below it is x's history, not a's, so a's two objects merge into {p:1, q:2}. The same rule as 010–017 with a scalar instead of null; typesafe/config 1.4.9 lets the 5 cut a's merge

a name without an extension is a basename: all of base.properties, base.json and base.conf exist, so all three are loaded and merged, properties first and HOCON last, so the .conf value wins where they overlap
a basename with only base.conf present loads just that file
a basename with only base.properties present loads it as Java properties, whose values are all strings

in a properties file a dotted key is a path, so a.b and a.c build an object at a; the spec's Java properties mapping says the object must always win when a key is both a value and a parent, whatever the order; values are strings
a .json file found through a basename is parsed as JSON and contributes its object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an unquoted value is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; ${} is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON has no trailing commas
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; the spec's own footing is that duplicate keys are invalid JSON (L194-195), so the second a is an error rather than an override
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON separates array elements with commas only; whitespace does not concatenate or separate
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an empty document is not JSON, although it is an empty HOCON object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON document included here must be an object; a bare number is neither an object nor valid as an included root
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a quoted string; a number cannot be a key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; in JSON a newline between fields does not stand in for the comma
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a plain string, not a path expression, so a.b stays a single key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON forbids a leading zero on a number. typesafe/config reads 01 as 1, the same leniency it shows in HOCON

x.txt has an extension, so it is not a basename to probe; it is a file adjacent to the including one and of the same type. The spec does not define what counts as an extension, and this row reads any dotted suffix as one. typesafe/config probes every name that does not end in .conf, .json or .properties as a basename and finds nothing
base.properties and base.json both exist; JSON is parsed next-to-last, after properties, so its value for a wins
base.json and base.conf both exist; HOCON is parsed last, after JSON, so its value for a wins
for a URL, file: included, only the exact URL is used and no extension is tried: inc does not exist, though inc.conf beside it does, so the include finds nothing and, not required, adds nothing
an absolute file: URL is read as given, its format taken from the extension of its path, .conf: {a: 1}
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; // and # comments are a HOCON extension, and JSON has none

the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON document has one array or object at the root, and a second object on the next line is trailing content, not a field and not a merge
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON string may not hold a raw control character, and a tab is one, so it must be written as \t

the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON whitespace is only space, tab, LF and CR, and the wider set with the no-break space 0x00A0 is defined for HOCON only (L167-172). typesafe/config treats a no-break space as whitespace in JSON too

the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON, whose whitespace has no BOM: the BOM-is-whitespace rule is HOCON's. RFC 8259 section 8.1 lets a JSON parser ignore a leading BOM or reject it, and this spec does not choose, so both pass
a file() argument is not interpreted relative to the including file, so the marker beside sub/inner.conf is not loaded; nothing of that name exists elsewhere and the include is ignored
the included file may contain substitutions like any other; typesafe/config refuses an include nested in a list when the included file is not fully resolved
an included key merges exactly as a duplicate key in one file would, so over.conf's a = null cuts a off from the a { x = 1 } above it, and its a { z = 3 } starts afresh: {a: {z: 3}}; pyhocon keeps x
the same with a scalar: over.conf's a = 2 replaces the object above, and a.z = 3 replaces the 2, so only z is left: {a: {z: 3}}
child.conf's a = bar hides the ${r} above it, and its a { m = 1 } replaces bar: a is {m: 1}, and ${r} is never merged in
substitutions in included files are looked up first relative to the root of the included file and only second relative to the root of the including configuration, so a.x wins over x

an included file may intend to refer to the application's root config, for example to get a value from the environment; the original path CONFORMANCE_HOME is looked up and falls back to the environment variable

an undefined ${?nope} means common.x.y is never created, so ${x.y} is not found at the fixed-up path and is looked up at the original path x.y. typesafe/config treats the vanished value as a miss that ends the lookup -- except in some root key orders (see 014); lightbend/config#863 falls back
the optional form of 009 falls back the same way; typesafe/config leaves a out instead (lightbend/config#863)
an undefined optional that would override keeps the previous value, so common.x.y is 9 and found at the fixed-up path; the original path is not consulted
an unrelated key that reads common.x must not change what common.a resolves to; in typesafe/config this input fails while the same input with the key named o24bbd resolves to 0 (lightbend/config#863)
a.x is present, set to null, so the lookup at the fixed-up path succeeds and the original path x is not consulted
a substitution in an included file is looked up first relative to the included file's root, here the list element, so ${y} finds y = 1 next to it; the spec makes no exception for a list
relative to the included file's root first: ${y} is the element's y = 1, not the including file's y = 2

a += 2 in a file included at k is a = ${?a} [2], fixed up to ${?k.a}; looking back, k.a has no earlier value, so the original path a is looked up as well and k.a appends to it. typesafe/config lets the self-reference end the lookup, the same for the long form, though it falls back for b = ${?a} [2]

a += 3 in child.conf looks for k.a first, which is not there, then for a from the root (L1010, as in 025): the text "", and += onto a value that is no list is an error (L731). typesafe/config treats the include's a as unrelated to the root's

b = ${?b} in child.conf has nothing below it at a.b, so it is as if a.b were not in the document, and the path is looked up from the root next (L1010, as in 025): b is {}, and so is a.b. typesafe/config drops a.b
whitespace inside the parentheses, outside the quotes, is allowed
an include stands where a field would, so the usual comma separates it from the field that follows
an include is separated from the field that follows by the usual comma, which only a newline may replace; on one line with neither, b is a stray token after the resource name

leaving out the separator before { changes nothing about the value: a { m = 2 } { n = 1 } is a : { m = 2 } { n = 1 }, two objects concatenated into one; typesafe/config and pyhocon read only the first object and reject the second
the same with a substitution after the object: a { m = 2 } ${x} is a : { m = 2 } ${x}, and the two objects merge; typesafe/config and pyhocon reject the substitution
the [] suffix collects CONFORMANCE_LIST_0, CONFORMANCE_LIST_1, ... until an index is missing, into a list of strings
with no CONFORMANCE_LIST_0 set, an optional ${?X[]} is undefined and the field is not created
indices are collected from 0 until one is missing, so with _0 and _2 set the list holds only the first
an element taken from the environment is a string, so 1 stays "1"
the [] suffix collects environment variables only, so the config key a_0 is not gathered and the optional substitution is undefined
the conversion should be done in a concatenation when a list is expected and an object with numeric keys is found, so the trailing object concatenates onto the array as elements x, y
the conversion should ignore any keys which do not parse as positive integers, so key "foo" is dropped and only "0" contributes to the resulting array

the conversion should sort by the integer value of each key and then build the array; missing indices such as "1" are eliminated rather than left as gaps, so keys "0" and "2" become a two-element array
the conversion ignores any keys which do not parse as positive integers, and "-1" is not a positive integer, so it is dropped and only key "0" contributes
an empty file does not begin with a square bracket or a curly brace, so it is parsed as if enclosed in {}: the empty object

the implicit {} wrap fires only when the file does not begin with a square bracket or curly brace, so a file starting with [ keeps its array root; the include section says so outright -- 'both JSON and HOCON allow arrays as root values in a document' (the reason an included file may not be one). typesafe/config has no array-rooted config at all and rejects the document as LIST rather than object.
an empty array is still an array root, and the wrap rule looks at the opening bracket, not at whether the document has content
a comment is ignored, so the file still begins with a square bracket and the {} wrap does not fire: the root is the array
leading whitespace does not trigger the {} wrap either, for the same reason as a leading comment
a file holding only a comment does not begin with a bracket or brace, so it is the empty object
a path that ends with a dot is invalid and should generate an error

a key may start with a number and run into +=: 3 and 1e are keys, and += appends to nothing: {"3": [[]], "1e": [1]}; typesafe/config reads + as part of the number and rejects it, pyhocon drops the brackets

the unquoted string include may not begin a path expression in a key: where an object key is expected, include is not read as a key at all and must be followed by a quoted resource name, so include.foo is an error. typesafe/config recognises the keyword only as a bare include token -- include.foo tokenizes as one unquoted string, so it is accepted as the path include.foo, while include = 42 is rejected under the very rule the spec states.
only the unquoted string include that begins a path expression in a key is special: include later in a key (foo.include) and a quoted "include" beginning one are ordinary path elements
inside an object, += desugars to a self-reference by the field's full path o.a; the appended element may itself be a substitution
b has no previous value, so b += 1 is b = ${?b} [1] with the optional part undefined: [1]. typesafe/config refuses += inside a list because its desugared path cannot name a list element
the self-reference += desugars to uses the full path of the field, o.p.a, even when the enclosing key was written as the path o.p

l += v is l = ${?l} [v]; the appended object holds a merge of an object and a substitution, which resolves inside the new list. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) for the same reason as array-and-object-concatenation/018
y.l += 3 overrides the y.l that the earlier concatenation defines, so its self-reference looks back at [1, 2]; typesafe/config yields [3] (lightbend/config#375)
c.x += 1 looks back at c.x, which ${d} gives, and the second += at the first: [1, 2], and d is left as it was (lightbend/config#177)
the self-reference in b += 2 refers to the b it overrides in the same object, 1, and += onto a value that is not a list is an error, in a list element as anywhere
the self-reference in b += 2 refers to the b it overrides in the same object, [1]: b is [1, 2], in a list element as anywhere. typesafe/config refuses an include or a self-reference inside a list

b.x += 2 is b.x = ${?b.x} [2], and it overrides the b.x = [1] that merges onto the object ${a} gives b, so it appends to [1]: [1, 2], as without b = ${a}; typesafe/config drops the 1 when the two fields are separate objects over a substitution, though it gets b { x = [1], x += 2 } right

the error twin of 012: y.l += 2 is y.l = ${?y.l} [2] and looks back at the l = 1 the earlier concatenation merged in, and a number before an array is an error just as in the long form; typesafe/config drops the earlier value and starts a fresh [2]

a.b += x is a { b = ${?a.b} [x] }, an object that replaces the number without merging, so the first += finds no a.b and starts [x], and the second appends to it: [x, y]; typesafe/config keeps only the last element, as it does after the null in 014

foo += b is foo = ${?foo} [b], and the previous value is an object with numeric keys; in that concatenation a list is expected, so the object converts to [a] and b is appended rather than += failing on a non-array
y's ${?b} leads back to y through b.c's ${y}, so it is nonexistent (L716) and y is [1]; ${y} is required and resolves to that, so b.c is [[1], 2]
as 022 with y written first: y is [1], b.c is [[1], 2]

e's last value reaches e again through c, so it is self-referential and looks back at the first e += ${?c}, whose own ${?c} leads back to e and is nonexistent: c is [] there, and keeps it, as a substitution is resolved once, so e is [[]]. Or c is an alias for the final e, every optional on the cycle nonexistent: [] both (also_valid), as in self-referential-examples/035 and 065
as 024 with c written first: c is [], e is [[]], or [] both (also_valid)

a's ${?b} leads back to a through b's ${?a}, and the other way round, so each is nonexistent (L716) whichever field is resolved first: both lists are empty, as for the list form in self-referential-examples/057. typesafe/config keeps the one it met second
as 026 with b written first: both []

d's ${?c} leads back to d through c's ${?d}, and the other way round, so both are nonexistent (L716): d is 1 next to nothing, the string "1" (substitutions/039), and c is []. typesafe/config resolves c's ${?d} to the number
as 028 with c written first: c is [], d is "1"

d.z += 5 is d.z = ${?d.z} [5], its ${?d.z} looking back at d.z's layer below, ${?a.k} (L719-745). That optional leads to a, whose a += ${d} leads back to d.z, so it is nonexistent (L716) and d.z is [5]. a copies d, so a is [{z: [5]}]: a substitution is resolved once (L884), and d.z is one value, the same in d and in a's copy of it, whichever field is resolved first
as the case before with a written first: d.z is [5] and a is [{z: [5]}]

a list merges with nothing, so any later value hides it and it is never evaluated; that the hiding object arrives through ${replacement} changes nothing, since the substitution is required and so either resolves or fails on its own. typesafe/config evaluates the hidden list (lightbend/config#865)

a reader of w.x must not change whether the hidden list is evaluated; only objects merge, so the object hides the list whatever else refers to it. typesafe/config fails here, yet resolves the same file with the reader named o24bbd (lightbend/config#865)

c.x is self-referential, and ${d} { ... } merges the object over d, so ${c.x} looks back at the overridden d.x, as with c : ${d} and c { x : ${c.x} [1, 2] } written as two fields; typesafe/config reports a cycle
three objects merged in one value, the last overriding both: ${c.x} looks back at what ${d} ${e} gives c.x, and ${e.z} is an ordinary forward reference; typesafe/config reports a cycle
an object with a substitution inside it is not self-referential, so ${a.hello} looks forward and finds the field the merged ${mixin} gives a; typesafe/config reports a cycle (lightbend/config#586)
${top.n} is not self-referential, so it looks forward, including at the field being defined: the merged top.n, 2, not x's 1; typesafe/config reports a cycle

as 035, through a path: inside p's look-back a is the earlier 1, which has no z, so p = "x"; a keeps the memoized 1 (expect) or is an alias for the final p (also_valid). typesafe/config gives a = "x", which is the second reading, though for 035 it takes the first

035 with a defined first: p's last value reaches p again through a, so the cycle is broken by looking back at p = 1, and p = "1x" whichever field is resolved first. a keeps the memoized 1 (expect) or is an alias for the final p (also_valid); an error is not allowed, the cycle can be broken

p's last value is an object, so it is not self-referential and ${a.q} looks forward: a is the merged p, and only its q is needed, which is 1. The same principle as 029, through an alias; there is no cycle to report
r needs v, v.x needs r: a cycle, and a cycle is a missing value for an optional substitution, so v.x is not created. v and r are both {}

${?a} inside a.n leads back to a.n through a, so it is as if it referred to a nonexistent value and a.n is {h: 0}; o is the final a.n, whichever field is resolved first: substitutions are memoized, so both have the same value
${?b} leads back to a.n through b = ${a}, so it is nonexistent and a.n is {h: 0}; b is a, and o is a.n, the same value everywhere. typesafe/config reports b's ${a} as unresolved

each optional leads back to the field it stands in, ${?a.t} through a and ${?f} through f, so each is as if it referred to a nonexistent value, whichever field is resolved first: f is "x" and a is y's {t: 1}
${?c} leads back to d through c = ${d}, so it is nonexistent and an empty string in the concatenation: d and c are "yes", in either order of the lines
e += ${?c} is e = ${?e} [${?c}]; ${?c} leads back to e through c = ${e}, so it is nonexistent and the element is not added: e and c are []
i = ${d} comes back to i through d.a = ${i.b}, so it is self-referential and looks back: ${i.b} sees i.b = 7. d is {a: 7}, and i is {b: 7} merged with it
p = ${a} comes back to p through a = [${p}], so it looks back at p = 1: a is [1] and p is a, [1], as 035 with the alias in a list
p's last value is an object, so it is not self-referential and ${a.q} looks forward through the alias a, resolving only q: r is 1, as 038 with a = ${p} written twice
${?x.y} leads back to x, so it is nonexistent and x is "5ms"; the list below is hidden by the string and never evaluated
a concatenation with a list in it is a list or an error, never an object, so the object after it does not merge with it and it is hidden: never evaluated, and c is {a: 1}

the second c comes back to itself through a, and has c = 2 below to look back at: while it is resolved the list is seen with c at 2, so c is [{c: 2}]. a : [${a}] is unbreakable only because nothing is below

unlike 022, the undefined optional sits one level down: it leaves out only bar, while the path w.bar still makes w an object, and that object hides the list, so ${does-not-exist} is never evaluated. typesafe/config evaluates a list hidden by an object that holds a substitution (lightbend/config#865)

the 1 under the list changes nothing: merging goes two values at a time, the object replaces the list without merging, so the list is hidden and ${does-not-exist} is never evaluated. typesafe/config resolves the same file without the 1, but keeps an unresolved list over a scalar as a delayed merge and evaluates it (lightbend/config#865)

b's ${?a} leads back to b through a = [${?b}], and a's ${?b} back to a through b, so each optional is as if it referred to a nonexistent value (L673, L716), whichever field is resolved first: both lists are empty. typesafe/config keeps the one it met second

b's last value reaches b again through a.f, so b is self-referential; a is an object and not self-referential, so the cycle is broken at b, by looking back at b = 1, and that resolves it: b = {f: 1}, not an error. a.f keeps the 1 it resolved to inside the look-back (expect) or is an alias for the final b (also_valid), as in 035; typesafe/config starts from a and reports a cycle

f's ${?a} is resolved to see whether it merges with the object over it, and reaches f again through a: from that layer f has nothing below (L659), so a's ${?f.z} finds nothing there, and keeps that, as a substitution is resolved once (L886): a is no field, as in 035 and 065. Or a is an alias for the final f.z, the object's 3 (also_valid)
x${?a} is text or an error, never an object, so the object over it hides it and it is never evaluated (L776): f is { z = 3 }, which ${?f} reaches without coming back to a

d's ${?c} leads back to d through c, and c's ${?d} back to c through d, so both are nonexistent (L716) whichever field is resolved first: d is [] and c, an optional with nothing behind it, is no field. typesafe/config keeps c as []

e's last value reaches e again through c, so it is self-referential and looks back at e = x${?c}, whose own ${?c} leads back to e and is nonexistent: c is "x" there, and keeps it, as a substitution is resolved once, so e is "xyx". Or c is an alias for the final e, the optionals on the cycle nonexistent: "xy" both (also_valid), as in 035
as 065 with c written first: c is "x", e is "xyx", or "xy" both (also_valid)

${r}x has text in it, so it is text or an error, never an object (L384): the object over it hides it, and it is never evaluated (L776), although r is an object and the concatenation would be an error. typesafe/config merges r into a

d.z is written twice, ${?a.k} then += ${?c}. Resolving a walks f, then d, and d.z is reached again from inside a's own look-back (L767): it is still a field with two layers, resolved as one, not a value. ${?a.k} leads back to d.z through a, f and d, so it is nonexistent (L716), ${?c} too, and d.z is []; a is [] with f appended (L731)

e's ${?f.k} leads back to e through f's ${e}, and f's ${?e} back to f through e's ${?f.k}: both are nonexistent (L716) whichever field is resolved first, so e is [y] and f is ${e}, [y]. A substitution is resolved once (L884-886): f's ${?e}, found nonexistent while e was resolved, stays nonexistent when f is resolved afterwards. typesafe/config calls the cycle an error
074 with f first: e is [y] and f is [y] again

b.k.k's ${?e} leads to e.k, whose ${?b} leads back into b, the object holding b.k.k: both optionals are on the cycle and nonexistent (L716), so e.k is no field and e is {}, and b.k.k is ${?d} appended to nothing, []. Whichever field is resolved first (077). typesafe/config concatenates e's {} with the list and fails
076 with b first: e is {} and b.k.k is [] again

a += ${o} is a = ${?a} [${o}], self-referential through ${?a}; the cycle through ${o} is broken by looking back, with o's a at its earlier value []: o = {a: [{a: []}]}, the implementation the spec sketches

${?r} is undefined, so the previous value of v.x remains, ${v}: a field referring to the object it is in, the a : { b : ${a} } the spec names an unbreakable cycle. typesafe/config sets the field aside and reads v as {}

n.a's ${?b} leads back to n.a through b = ${n.a}, so it is nonexistent (L716), and what is left of n.a is ${n}, a field referring to the object it is in: a cycle no look-back breaks (L688-691, as in 008). typesafe/config gives {} for both

it is invalid for arrays or objects to appear in a string value concatenation; typesafe/config accepts this one silently and discards the trailing x, losing data with no diagnostic, while erroring on the same pair in the other order
the same rule for arrays; typesafe/config again accepts and discards the trailing x, where it errors when the scalar comes first
an array may not appear in a string value concatenation, with or without whitespace between them; typesafe/config silently drops suffix (lightbend/config#862)
the same rule for an object followed directly by text; typesafe/config silently drops suffix (lightbend/config#862)
text between two arrays makes a concatenation of array, string and array, which is invalid; typesafe/config drops the text and concatenates the arrays (lightbend/config#862)
a substitution in a string concatenation becomes text the way a number written there does, as written: 1e5 and 1.50, not 100000.0 and 1.5

a self-reference with no earlier value is undefined "exactly as if the substitution referenced a path not found in the document", and such a path is searched for in the environment, so the field reads the variable of its own name; typesafe/config reports a cycle, which the spec rules out ("undefined" rather than "intractable cycle")

if ${?foo} refers to itself "it's as if it referred to a nonexistent value", and a value not present in the configuration is searched for in the environment, so the field is created from the variable instead of disappearing
the path inside ${} has the syntax of an object key, and whitespace before the first and after the last element of a key is discarded, so ${ b } is ${b}
a is a number, so a.x names nothing; a required substitution to an undefined path is an error
the same path with the optional form: undefined, so the field is not created

a path names object fields only, so b.0 does not reach into the list b even though it has an element at index 0; the optional substitution is undefined and a is not created. The list is still unresolved when the lookup happens, which is what makes an implementation look inside it
only whitespace before the ? is forbidden; after it the path follows and its leading whitespace is discarded as in any key
${?n}01 is a concatenation of two parts, so it is a string (042), and 01 is no JSON number anyway: "01". typesafe/config and pyhocon drop the undefined part and read the number 1

JSON reads only the 0 of 01 as a number, a zero is not followed by digits; what follows is text after the number, as 10.0bar is the number 10.0 then bar (unquoted-strings.9), and a number keeps the text it was written with in a concatenation, so the value is the string "01". typesafe/config reads the number 1.

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON requires a digit before the decimal point, so -.33 is no number; it holds no forbidden character and its initial characters parse as no number, so it is the unquoted string "-.33", as .33 is (unquoted-strings/018). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -0.33; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads the string

-.33e+1 has no integer part, so it is no JSON number, and as text it would hold a +, a forbidden character outside the exponent of a number; without the + it is text (032). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it, on the reserved +
JSON requires a digit after the decimal point, so the number is 1 and the dot is text after it: the string "1.". typesafe/config reads it as 1, and lightbend/config#861 leaves it so on purpose
the same with an exponent after the dot: the number is -1 and .e3 is text after it, the string "-1.e3"; typesafe/config reads it as -1000 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)

JSON forbids leading zeros after the minus sign as well, so the number is -0 and 033 text after it; a number keeps its text in a concatenation, so the value is the string "-0033". typesafe/config reads it as -33 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
NaN is not a JSON number, so the bare token is an unquoted string
number formats match JSON, which has no size limit, so an integer past 2^63 is still a number; typesafe/config makes it a string (lightbend/config#801, ekrich/sconfig#631)
a JSON \u escape is exactly four hex digits, and + is not one; typesafe/config reads +041 as hex 41, A (lightbend/config#884, ekrich/sconfig#623)
a JSON \u escape is four ASCII hex digits; Arabic-Indic digits are not, though typesafe/config parses them as 0041, A (lightbend/config#884, ekrich/sconfig#623)
JSON allows a sign in the exponent, so -0.33e+1 is a number, -3.3; the + that unquoted text may not hold is part of the number here

the same as 010 with an exponent: -.33e1 has no integer part and is no JSON number, and it holds no forbidden character, so it is the string "-.33e1"; with a + in the exponent it is an error (011). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads the string

number formats are JSON's, where 08080, 01.5 and 0. are no numbers: JSON reads 0, then the rest is text after it, so all three are the strings as written, as 01 is (009). typesafe/config reads 8080, 1.5 and 0; pyhocon 8080 and 1.5

files must be valid UTF-8, and that holds for the whole file: a byte that is never UTF-8 (0xFF) inside a comment makes the file invalid, although the comment's text is ignored. typesafe/config decodes it to U+FFFD and drops the comment.
worked example: truefoo parses as the boolean token true followed by the unquoted string foo, because its initial characters parse as true

-. begins no JSON number, so -.33e+1x is text from its first character, and its + is a forbidden character there: an error, as -.33e+1 is (unchanged-from-json/011). typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 read the string; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it
a lone carriage return is whitespace but not a newline, so 1 b concatenates and the second = is a stray token
